:::{#thm-rank-transpose}
#### Fundamental theorem of ranks

For any $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})
= \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}})
= \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A})
= \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \tp{\matr{A}}).
$$

In particular, the largest number of linearly independent rows of $\matr{A}$
equals the largest number of linearly independent columns.

:::

::: proof

**$\operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}) = \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})$.**
Both matrices have $n$ columns,
and $\mathcal{N}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}) = \mathcal{N}(\matr{A})$ (@thm-null-gram),
so they have the same nullity (@def-nullity).
Then

$$
\ba
\operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A})
&= n - \operatorname{nullity}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-nullity)}
\\
&= n - \operatorname{nullity}(\matr{A})
&& \text{(equal null spaces)}
\\
&= \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}).
&& \text{(@thm-rank-nullity)}
\ea
$$

**$\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \tp{\matr{A}}) = \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}})$.**
Apply the previous step to the $n \times m$ matrix $\tp{\matr{A}}$,
using $\tp{(\tp{\matr{A}})} = \matr{A}$.

**Chain the inequalities.**

$$
\ba
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})
&= \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A})
&& \text{(first step)}
\\
&\le \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}})
&& \text{(@thm-rank-product, with } \tp{\matr{A}} \text{ on the left)}
\\
&= \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A} \tp{\matr{A}})
&& \text{(second step)}
\\
&\le \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}).
&& \text{(@thm-rank-product, with } \matr{A} \text{ on the left)}
\ea
$$

The chain starts and ends at $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})$,
so every quantity in it equals $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})$.
The columns of $\tp{\matr{A}}$ are the rows of $\matr{A}$,
which gives the statement about rows.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-transpose}
#### Four equal ranks

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space, $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = 1$ (@exm-rank-dim).
Its transpose
$\tp{\matr{A}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ -2 & -6 \\ -2 & -6 \end{bmatrix}$
has second column $3$ times its first, so its rank is $1$.
$\tp{\matr{A}} \matr{A}$ in @exm-null-gram has every row a multiple of $(1, -2, -2)$,
so its rank is $1$ too, and

$$
\matr{A} \tp{\matr{A}}
= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \cd 1 + (-2)(-2) + (-2)(-2) & 1 \cd 3 + (-2)(-6) + (-2)(-6) \\
3 \cd 1 + (-6)(-2) + (-6)(-2) & 3 \cd 3 + (-6)(-6) + (-6)(-6) \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 27 \\ 27 & 81 \end{bmatrix},
$$

whose second column is $3$ times its first, so its rank is $1$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#cor-rank-bound}
#### The rank is at most the smaller dimension

For any $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$,
$\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) \le \min\cb{m, n}$.

:::

::: proof

$\matr{A}$ has $n$ columns,
so at most $n$ of them are linearly independent,
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) \le n$ (@def-rank).
Likewise $\tp{\matr{A}}$ has $m$ columns,
so $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = \operatorname{rank}(\tp{\matr{A}}) \le m$
(@thm-rank-transpose).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-bound}
#### A $2 \times 3$ matrix has rank at most $2$

By @cor-rank-bound, every $2 \times 3$ matrix has rank at most $\min\cb{2, 3} = 2$,
even though it has $3$ columns.
The matrix
$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
of @rem-full-column-rank-shape reaches that bound:
its first two columns $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ are linearly independent,
so its rank is $2$.

:::
